::: {.why}
Day 117 neutralised weights after the fact; neutralising the signal itself changes what the forecast is, and the two are not equivalent when the sizing is nonlinear.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Neutralise a signal by cross-sectional regression against exposures and say what the residual is a forecast of.
- Report the difference between neutralising at the signal level and at the portfolio level for the same signal.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Add `neutralise` to qlib/signals/transforms.py: cross-sectionally regress the signal on the exposure matrix on each date and keep the residual. Then run the same signal three ways, unneutralised, signal-neutralised and portfolio-neutralised, and report Sharpe, factor loadings and turnover for each.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Say what you gave up: the residual signal is orthogonal to the exposures you removed, which means any genuine forecasting power that ran through those exposures is gone. Quantify it by reporting how much of the original signal's variance the neutralisation removed.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Decide and record the policy for the book: which exposures every signal is neutralised against by default, and the reason.
:::
:::

## The running strategy

::: {.project}
Signals are neutralised at the signal level against a standard exposure set declared once for the whole book, with the variance removed reported per signal so the cost of neutralising is visible.
:::
